prompt.context: The railway company of Spain (RENFE), a former monopoly, is now opening to competition. RENFE has been divided into two separate companies: RENFE (train operation) and ADIF (company that manages the tracks, train stations and traffic control). A friend of yours has 90M € and has approached you for advice on starting a new train operation company to compete against the new RENFE. In particular, he wants to start by opening a new high speed train route between Madrid and Barcelona.
prompt.question: Should your friend go ahead and launch the business?

clarifying_info.q: How does our service compare to RENFE on price?
How does our service compare to RENFE on efficiency?
clarifying_info.a: We are more efficiently run — RENFE is a former monopoly and very inefficient.

clarifying_info.q: How does our service compare to RENFE on travel time?
How does our service compare to RENFE on convenience?
clarifying_info.a: Equally convenient — we use the same stations and tracks.

clarifying_info.q: How does our service compare to air travel on price?
How does our service compare to air travel on time?
clarifying_info.a: About equal overall — check-in time, luggage pick-up, delays, and traffic mean either can be faster depending on circumstances.

clarifying_info.q: How does our service compare to air travel on convenience?
clarifying_info.a: We are more convenient — none of the friction factors that apply to air travel.

clarifying_info.q: What are the operating parameters (hours, trips per day, fleet)?
clarifying_info.a: Travel time between Madrid and Barcelona is 4 hours. Trains run from 8am until 10pm. We can run two round trips per day. We need 3 active trains plus 1 backup, so 4 trains total and 4 trips per day.
30M € per train (4 trains = 120M € total capital investment).

clarifying_info.q: What are annual operations and maintenance costs?
What is the train capacity and fare/occupancy data?
clarifying_info.a: Each train holds 500 people. At 40 €, occupancy is 95%. At 50 €, occupancy is 80%. At 60 €, occupancy is 60%.

exhibits.title: Case Page (p88)
exhibits.shows: The full case page including the stem and Phase 1 overview text as printed in the casebook
exhibits.data: Case stem text; competitor comparison table (Us vs. RENFE, Us vs. air travel)

framework: Market attractiveness: size, growth, competitive intensity (RENFE vs. air vs. new entrant)
Competitive positioning: price, time, convenience vs. each competitor
Revenue model: ticket pricing optimization (price × occupancy × capacity), ancillary revenue streams
Cost structure: capex (trains), opex (marketing, operations/maintenance, personnel, IT)
Profitability & payback: annual profit vs. 10-year investment recovery requirement
Strategic options: leasing, JV, ancillary revenue to improve economics if base case is borderline

questions.prompt: Phase 1 — Industry overview: How does the new venture stack up against its two main competitors?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify RENFE and air travel as the two competitors and compare on price, time, and convenience. Strong answer: new entrant is cheaper and more convenient than both; time is roughly equal to RENFE and roughly equal to air when accounting for check-in, luggage, delays, and traffic. Conclusion: viable market opportunity exists, worth analyzing profitability.

questions.prompt: Phase 2 — Business overview: What are the main revenue streams and cost categories?
questions.guidance: Revenue: tickets are the primary driver; ancillary revenue (ads on trains, food and drinks) exists but is set aside for calculations. Costs: capex (train purchase), marketing, operations and maintenance, personnel, IT. Candidate should be organized and MECE in listing costs.

questions.prompt: Phase 3a — Optimal ticket price: Given capacity 500 and the three price/occupancy options, which ticket price maximizes revenue per trip?
questions.guidance: Candidate multiplies occupancy rate × capacity × ticket price for each scenario and picks the highest. The 50 € price point is optimal.

math.setup: Revenue per trip = occupancy rate × capacity × ticket price
math.answer: Set ticket price at 50 €, yielding 20,000 € revenue per trip.

questions.prompt: Phase 3b — Annual profit: Using the 50 € price point, calculate annual operating profit (costs stated are per operating train; only 3 trains operate on average).
questions.guidance: Annual revenue = 365 days × 4 trips/day × 20,000 €/trip. Annual costs = 25M € (15M marketing + 10M operations) per train × 3 operating trains. The backup (4th) train's operating costs are excluded since it is not in regular service. Total operating profit = revenue per train × 3 − total costs × 3.

math.setup: Annual revenue per train = 365 × 4 trips × 20,000 €; annual costs per train = 25M €
steps: Total operating profit (3 trains): 4.2M × 3 = 12.6M € per year
math.answer: 12.6M € annual operating profit across the 3 active trains.

questions.prompt: Phase 3c — Payback check: The company has only 10 years to recover its investment. Can it do so?
questions.guidance: Total capex = 4 trains × 30M = 120M €. At 12.6M €/year profit, payback takes ~9.5 years. This barely squeaks under 10 years and is very tight — essentially borderline. The friend started with only 90M € so the 120M capex alone exceeds available capital, making the investment infeasible without additional financing.

math.setup: Payback period = total capex / annual operating profit
math.answer: Payback ≈ 9.5 years — barely within 10-year limit, but capex (120M €) exceeds available capital (90M €), making the deal non-viable as structured.

brainstorming.prompt: What options could your friend consider to make the business more profitable or feasible?

categories.name: Capital structure
ideas: Lease trains instead of buying (converts 120M € capex to annual opex, preserving capital)
Joint venture with a foreign operator that has excess rolling stock capacity
Seek debt financing or equity partners to bridge the 30M € capital gap

categories.name: Revenue enhancement
ideas: Advertising on trains and in stations
Premium/business class seating tiers with higher fares
Loyalty program to increase repeat ridership
Ancillary luggage or bike storage fees

categories.name: Cost reduction
ideas: Negotiate volume discounts on train purchase or maintenance contracts
Share ADIF infrastructure costs with other operators
Optimize staffing schedules to reduce labor cost per trip

categories.name: Market expansion
ideas: Add additional high-demand routes once Madrid-Barcelona is proven
Increase frequency if demand supports it
Target corporate travel accounts for guaranteed volume

recommendation: Do NOT invest under the current circumstances: the 120M € capex exceeds the friend's 90M € capital, and the 9.5-year payback leaves virtually no margin for error within the 10-year window.
However, the competitive positioning is attractive — the new entrant is cheaper and more convenient than both RENFE and air travel, so the underlying market opportunity is real.
risks: Capital shortfall of 30M € means the friend cannot self-fund the full fleet
Any revenue shortfall or cost overrun eliminates the thin payback margin
RENFE may respond aggressively on price once competition begins
Regulatory changes or ADIF access disputes could increase operating costs
next_steps: Explore train leasing to convert capex to opex and bring investment within the 90M € budget
Evaluate a JV with a foreign operator that provides trains in exchange for revenue share
Model ancillary revenue (food, ads, premium seating) to see if total economics improve materially
Conduct detailed demand study to validate the 80% occupancy assumption at 50 €
